p.docTitle: Report of the Plenary of the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services on the work of its twelfth session

division.heading: Opening of the session

content.p: The twelfth session of the Plenary of the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services (IPBES) was held at the Manchester Central Convention Complex, in Manchester, United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland, from 3 to 8 February 2026.
Following a musical performance, the session was opened at 9.55 a.m. by the Chair of IPBES, David Obura, who welcomed participants and delivered an opening statement.

Opening statements were also delivered by Emma Reynolds, Secretary of State for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs of the United Kingdom; Kaveh Zahedi, Assistant Director General and Director of the Office of Climate Change, Biodiversity and Environment, Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), speaking on behalf of the four United Nations organizations supporting IPBES, namely FAO, the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) and the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO); Astrid Schomaker, Executive Secretary, Convention on Biological Diversity; Inger Andersen, Executive Director of UNEP; and Luthando Dziba, IPBES Executive Secretary.

In his opening remarks, the Chair thanked Ms. Reynolds and her team for their gracious efforts in organizing the session. He recalled that the mandate of IPBES was to synthesize and distil knowledge, taking in multiple world views, to enable decision makers to make the best possible choices, thereby affecting the fates of nature and people, which were interlinked.

The Plenary would engage in important work at its twelfth session, including on the methodological assessment of the impact and dependence of business on biodiversity and nature’s contributions to people (business and biodiversity assessment). Businesses, as engines of the economic sectors that mediated the ways that people made use of natural resources and biodiversity, would need to engage in a transformation towards sustainability in which Governments would play a vital enabling role. The assessment synthesized the many tools and pathways available and would assist businesses in all countries in working with, and not against, nature and people. At the current session, work would also be done on planning the activities of IPBES on building capacity, strengthening knowledge foundations, supporting policy and improving the effectiveness of the Platform, as well as in relation to its work during the final three years of the rolling work programme up to 2030. He asked participants to consider, during the upcoming intersessional period, how best to leverage the huge body of excellent work contained in IPBES assessments and to maximize its accessibility with a view to supporting Governments and key actors, possibly through lighter and more agile output formats such as synthesis reports and technical papers. Finally, he emphasized the crucial work of the contact group on budget, which would lay the foundation for improving the security of financial contributions, and noted that it was critical for the global community to support and expand the work of IPBES for the sake of better futures for all.

Ms. Reynolds, welcoming participants to Manchester, delivered a message from King Charles III underscoring the vital importance of nature as the ultimate foundation of societies and economies and recalling that it was under severe threat, especially as the triple planetary crisis of biodiversity loss, climate change and pollution was advancing at a pace that far outstripped the planet’s ability to cope. The best available science could help to inform decisions and actions to steward nature and restore it for future generations, and, through its assessments, IPBES had successfully brought together knowledge from world-leading scientists, Indigenous Peoples, local communities, citizens and Governments. King Charles expressed the hope that the business and biodiversity assessment would help to shape concrete action for years to come, including with regard to leveraging public and private sector funds to close the biodiversity funding gap of approximately $700 billion.

In her statement, Ms. Reynolds underlined the urgent need for collective action and, recalling the thematic assessment of the underlying causes of biodiversity loss and the determinants of transformative change and options for achieving the 2050 Vision for Biodiversity (transformative change assessment), she highlighted the need for a whole-of-society approach to addressing the biodiversity crisis. Momentum was building, as countries restored wetlands and forests, communities revived degraded landscapes, and businesses increased their investments in nature. Sound policy had to be built on sound evidence and up-to-date science, which was precisely what IPBES had been established to provide. Finally, she highlighted the opportunities for businesses, which were increasingly recognizing their dependence on nature, proving that nature-positive investment worked, and sending out a clear message that nature was fundamental to their interests. The business and biodiversity assessment would be a key tool to support businesses in taking further action. The science was already in place, as were the relevant frameworks and willing partners in government, academia and industry; what was needed now was urgent, collective and sustained action.

In his statement, Mr. Zahedi noted that the twelfth session was a milestone, being the tenth session held since the establishment of the collaborative partnership arrangement between IPBES and the four United Nations organizations that supported it. That partnership had been an integral part of the work of IPBES over the past decade. The organizations had provided staff, funding and technical support; worked on inclusive and rigorous assessments; and had striven to bring IPBES findings into global negotiations. Countries had applied knowledge from IPBES in their national policies, national biodiversity strategies and action plans, and monitoring systems, with support from initiatives such as the Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services Network, Capacity Development for Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services Experts, and the United Nations Biodiversity Lab. The organizations’ data platforms and global assessments supported the objectives of the partnership in many ways, including through the FAO data platforms and global assessments on fisheries, genetic resources and forests, the UNESCO Ocean Biodiversity Information System and Sites Navigator, the UNDP Nature Pledge and many data platforms hosted by UNEP.

Such collaboration mattered more than ever, as current challenges such as food insecurity and malnutrition, biodiversity loss, climate change and growing inequalities were systemic and interconnected. Those crises were a threat to lives and livelihoods everywhere, and they demanded science-based, evidence-driven, inclusive solutions backed by multilateral processes. Biodiversity was central to those solutions, as healthy ecosystems, species and genetic diversity underpinned food security, climate resilience and human well-being. The work of IPBES was crucial, as it delivered trusted, policy-relevant evidence that provided the clarity and credibility that financial institutions, Governments and development partners needed to align financial flows with global sustainability goals. Nevertheless, science alone was not enough; turning knowledge into transformative action required political uptake, adequate financing and inclusive governance. Through collective efforts, the business and biodiversity assessment would also help to catalyse private sector engagement on biodiversity. Paying tribute to the outstanding work of IPBES and the thousands of experts who had contributed their time and knowledge to it over the past decade, he reaffirmed the United Nations partners’ commitment to working with IPBES to ensure that its work continued to inform decisions on biodiversity, food security, nutrition and sustainable development for present and future generations.

In her statement, Ms. Schomaker noted that the rigorous science that IPBES provided as a public good would be needed more than ever in 2026, in particular during the global review on collective progress in the implementation of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework. She expressed deep appreciation to IPBES for its vital contribution to the collective endeavour to halt and reverse biodiversity loss, and for serving as a beacon of knowledge at a time when science and knowledge were under strain. The long history of cooperation between the secretariats of the Convention on Biological Diversity and IPBES reflected the way in which the two intergovernmental processes mutually supported each other in pursuit of common objectives. Parties to the Convention had a great interest in drawing on IPBES assessments and findings to inform recommendations and policy actions under the Convention; however, the highly technical nature of some of the scientific language used could make it difficult to translate key messages into policy. Clear summaries and more accessible framing would strengthen the bridge between science and policy, enabling parties to use the findings even more effectively. Discussions at the current session of the external part of the midterm review under the rolling work programme up to 2030, and how to implement the recommendations emanating from it, would provide a perfect occasion to reflect on ways to create actionable biodiversity science for policymakers and to account for the needs of end users.

With regard to the business and biodiversity assessment, she noted the crucial importance of clarifying that biodiversity loss was not merely an environmental issue, but posed a serious threat to economic systems, livelihoods, business profitability and societal resilience. Biodiversity was never a marginal issue in any type of business; it lay at the crux of what made companies thrive or flounder. In relation to target 15 of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, on reducing the negative impacts of business on biodiversity, she said that businesses needed to assess and disclose biodiversity-related risks and impacts not only in order to better understand the centrality of biodiversity for sourcing, operations, value chains and business models, but also to take action to transform business models and to reduce negative and increase positive biodiversity impacts. The assessment therefore made a timely contribution to the implementation of the Framework; without the engagement of the private sector, the 2030 targets were merely aspirations. At the same time, simply calling on businesses to do their part was not sufficient; they would need support in measuring impacts and dependencies, as well as an enabling environment that provided the right incentives to move from analysis and disclosure to changing their behaviour towards more nature-positive, nature-regenerative impacts. In closing, she expressed the hope that the assessment would contribute to economy-wide transformative change and that, with civil society mobilization, underpinned by science and a suitable policy framework, it would be possible not only to live in harmony with nature, but to thrive with nature.

In a statement delivered via video message, Ms. Andersen welcomed participants and noted that although they were gathering at a time of deep global fragmentation and uncertainty, science remained as one truth that could not be negotiated, delayed or compromised. That unequivocal nature of scientific evidence, along with the tangible environmental effects currently unfolding, made the work of IPBES more vital than ever. Businesses were increasingly feeling those effects – from disrupted supply chains and rising insurance losses to stranded assets and food and water insecurity – and nature loss had become a systemic economic risk. The business and biodiversity assessment was therefore both urgent and necessary. Although business leaders had clearly recognized extreme weather events, biodiversity loss and ecosystem collapse as leading long-term global risks, the role of nature in the global economy was still profoundly undervalued. The business and biodiversity assessment would deliver authoritative evidence on how businesses depended on nature, how they affected it and what that meant for risk, resilience and long-term value creation. That evidence would strengthen accountability and transparency, help to inform finance and investment decisions, allow governments to provide the right enabling conditions for sustainable business practices, and empower consumers, civil society, Indigenous Peoples and many local communities in their engagement with businesses.

Ms. Andersen noted that the twelfth session would also afford participants an opportunity to reflect on the work of IPBES to date. The business and biodiversity assessment would be the fourteenth IPBES assessment to be delivered, and work on three further assessments was ongoing. Participants would hold important discussions on the future work programme and examine not only how IPBES generated knowledge, but also how assessment findings could be translated into real-world action with far-reaching impacts. In closing, she reaffirmed that UNEP, together with FAO, UNDP and UNESCO, stood ready to support turning the outcomes of the meeting into tangible change in order to align economic decision-making in the public and private sectors with environmental reality and deliver lasting benefits for people and the planet.

In his opening remarks, Mr. Dziba expressed his sincere appreciation to his predecessor, Anne Larigauderie, and to Neville Ash, who had served as officer-in-charge following her retirement. The business and biodiversity assessment would clearly demonstrate the relevance of IPBES work for decision-making across the whole of society, as it would enable not only those in Government but also those in the private and financial sectors and in civil society to strengthen their contributions towards the 2050 Vision for Biodiversity and other related global goals. The work under way on other assessments was additional evidence that IPBES was on track not only to deliver crucial knowledge and inspiration to support existing goals and targets but also to provide the scientific foundation needed by the many processes that were currently shaping the global biodiversity agenda beyond 2030. Discussions during the current session would provide an important opportunity to think creatively in planning the future of IPBES itself, ensuring that all the Platform’s assessments, once completed, achieved the maximum possible reach and impact at the global level.

In closing, he thanked the members of the IPBES community for their enthusiasm, encouragement and unwavering commitment to the work of the Platform in 2025. In particular, he expressed appreciation to the Government of Germany for its continued generosity and support, including by hosting the secretariat, and to the four United Nations system partners. Welcoming the fact that more than 2,600 participants had registered for the current session, of whom more than 1,500 were attending in person, he noted with satisfaction that more than 500 delegates had registered to participate in the stakeholder day that had been held on 2 February 2026.
A video was shown, welcoming participants to Manchester and highlighting key IPBES events and progress since the eleventh session.

The representatives of Ghana on behalf of the Group of African States; Indonesia on behalf of the Group of Asia-Pacific States; Bosnia and Herzegovina on behalf of the Group of Eastern European States; Colombia on behalf of the Group of Latin American and Caribbean States; Cyprus on behalf of the European Union and its member States; and Switzerland, speaking also on behalf of Australia, Canada, Iceland, Israel, Japan, New Zealand, Norway and the United Kingdom, made general statements in which they spoke of the progress of IPBES to date; welcomed the appointment of Mr. Dziba as Executive Secretary; highlighted challenges faced and activities carried out in relation to IPBES; underscored the importance of the continued scientific integrity of IPBES work; commended the work of the experts on the business and biodiversity assessment; and outlined their expectations for the current session and the future work of IPBES. The representative of Armenia delivered a statement in the country’s capacity as President-designate of the seventeenth meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity, due to be held in Yerevan in October 2026, and the representative of France delivered a statement in which she announced her Government’s pledge to contribute an additional €300,000 to the trust fund of the Platform. The representatives of two stakeholders – the Open-ended Network of IPBES Stakeholders and the International Indigenous Forum on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services – also delivered statements.
The Chair announced that the Bureau had elected Bishwa Nath Oli (Nepal) to serve as Rapporteur of the twelfth session.

In response to a question from one representative regarding the legal implications of the proposed withdrawal of the United States from the Platform, the Legal Adviser said that, as membership of IPBES was entirely voluntary and as the Platform was not a treaty body, it was sufficient for a member to send notification of its withdrawal to the secretariat. The Chair took note of the concerns expressed by the same representative regarding the implications of the withdrawal of technical, scientific and financial contributions of the United States from the work of the Platform, which, he said, were matters that were likely to arise in the discussions of the two working groups at the current session.

subdivision.heading: Election of officers

content.p: Introducing the item, the Chair recalled that, at its ninth session, held in Bonn, Germany, from 3 to 9 July 2022, the Plenary had elected 25 members to a Multidisciplinary Expert Panel for a term of office of three years, in accordance with the rules of procedure of the Plenary. He noted that, in September 2025, Mr. Dziba had resigned from the Panel and had been succeeded by the alternate member from the region, John Kazembe (Malawi). The term of office of all members of the Panel would end at the closure of the current session of the Plenary and a new Panel would be elected for a term of three years, running from the closure of the current session to the closure of the fifteenth session.

The Chair also recalled that, in accordance with rule 27 of the rules of procedure, the secretariat had invited members of IPBES to submit to the secretariat written nominations with accompanying curricula vitae of nominees to the Panel by 30 September 2025. The list of names and the curricula vitae of the nominees, together with the name of the country making each nomination, was available on the IPBES website and, for those nominations that had been received by the deadline, was also set out in document IPBES/12/INF/2. Of the 47 nominations received, two had been submitted after the deadline and one, from Sweden, had been withdrawn. He noted that, in accordance with rule 27, paragraph 2, of the rules of procedure, the Plenary could accept late nominations at its discretion. All nominees had submitted conflict-of-interest forms in accordance with rule 3, paragraph 1, of the implementation procedures of the conflict-of-interest policy, as set out in annex II to decision IPBES-3/3. The Committee on Conflicts of Interest had reviewed the submissions and had determined that none of the nominees had a conflict of interest.

Furthermore, the Chair recalled that the roles of Panel member and assessment expert were incompatible. In the event that the Plenary elected a candidate who was involved in an ongoing IPBES assessment as an author, the candidate would have to resign from their role as author.

division.heading: Admission of observers

content.p: Introducing the item, the Chair recalled that, at its eleventh session, the Plenary had decided that the interim procedure for the admission of observers to sessions of the Plenary, as described in paragraph 22 of the report of the first session of the Plenary (IPBES/1/12) and applied at its second to eleventh sessions, would be applied at its twelfth session. In accordance with that interim procedure, the observers admitted to the previous sessions of the Plenary, as listed in part I of the annex to document IPBES/12/INF/3/Rev.1, were among those admitted to the current session. Part II of that annex contained a list of 85 organizations recommended by the Bureau for admission as new observers to the current session of the Plenary, while part III contained a list of 30 organizations not recommended for admission. The Plenary agreed to welcome the new observers, as recommended by the Bureau, to the twelfth session of the Plenary.

The Chair also recalled that, at previous sessions of the Plenary, diverging opinions had been expressed regarding the procedure for the admission of observers, as contained in paragraphs 14 to 17 of the draft policy and procedures for the admission of observers set out in the annex to document IPBES/12/3.

As opinions on the matter had not changed, the Plenary decided that the Plenary, at its thirteenth session, would continue to use the interim procedure for the admission of observers to sessions of the Plenary, as described in paragraph 22 of the report of the first session of the Plenary and applied at its second to twelfth sessions, on the understanding that observers admitted to its first to twelfth sessions would be among those admitted to its thirteenth session.

division.heading: Report of the Executive Secretary on progress in the implementation of the rolling work programme of the Platform up to 2030

content.p: Introducing the item, the Chair recalled that, in its decision IPBES-7/1, the Plenary had adopted the rolling work programme of IPBES for the period up to 2030. In its decision IPBES-11/1, it had requested the Executive Secretary to provide a report on progress in the implementation of the work programme to the Plenary at its twelfth session. The Executive Secretary, in consultation with the Multidisciplinary Expert Panel and the Bureau, had developed, for consideration by the Plenary, a report on progress in the implementation of the rolling work programme up to 2030 (IPBES/12/4). Additional information was set out in documents IPBES/12/INF/4 on the institutional arrangements established for the provision of technical support for the implementation of the work programme; IPBES/12/INF/6 on progress in the preparation of the methodological assessment on monitoring biodiversity and nature’s contributions to people (monitoring assessment), the methodological assessment of integrated biodiversity-inclusive spatial planning and ecological connectivity (spatial planning and connectivity assessment), and the second global assessment of biodiversity and ecosystem services; IPBES/12/INF/7 on the guide on the production of assessments; IPBES/12/INF/8 on the implementation of the conflict-of-interest policy; IPBES/12/INF/10 on work related to building capacity; IPBES/12/INF/11 on data and knowledge management; IPBES/12/INF/12 on a data and knowledge management policy and code of practice on the use of artificial intelligence; IPBES/12/INF/13 on knowledge generation catalysis; IPBES/12/INF/14 on enhanced recognition of and work with Indigenous and local knowledge systems; IPBES/12/INF/15 on advanced work on policy instruments, policy support tools and methodologies; IPBES/12/INF/16 on advanced work on scenarios and models of biodiversity and ecosystem functions and services; IPBES/12/INF/17 on strengthened communication; IPBES/12/INF/18 on strengthened engagement of stakeholders; and IPBES/12/INF/19 on engagement with the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC).

The Executive Secretary presented his report on progress in the implementation of the rolling work programme up to 2030 according to its six objectives, with another representative of the secretariat outlining communication activities. The Executive Secretary also gave a brief overview of the staffing situation within the secretariat and the implementation of the conflict-of-interest policy.

Co-Chairs of the monitoring assessment, the spatial planning and connectivity assessment and the second global assessment of biodiversity and ecosystem services delivered presentations on the development and implementation of those assessments. Each presentation provided information on the context and scope of the assessment; the team involved in work on the assessment; the structure of the assessment; progress made to date; and the steps and timeline for the completion of the assessment and consideration by the Plenary.
The Chair of IPCC presented an overview of the elements of the work of IPCC that were relevant to IPBES and of collaboration between IPCC and IPBES.
The Plenary took note of the information provided and welcomed the work carried out.

division.heading: Financial and budgetary arrangements for the Platform

content.p: The Executive Secretary provided an overview of the financial and budgetary arrangements for the Platform as set out in a note by the secretariat on the matter (IPBES/12/5) and a note by the secretariat on the detailed cost of the implementation of the work programme (IPBES/12/INF/9).

The Chair echoed the appreciation expressed by the Executive Secretary to countries and private sector donors that had contributed to the trust fund of the Platform, as well as to the countries and organizations that had provided in-kind or other support to IPBES, and to the many experts around the world who had devoted their time, free of charge, to the work of the Platform, thereby providing the largest in-kind contribution to IPBES. He noted that there was, nevertheless, an urgent need for additional national contributions for 2026 and subsequent years in order to bridge the $2.5 million gap between the Platform’s average annual income and expenditure, in particular given the planned withdrawal of the United States from the Platform, and he therefore invited those Governments that had not yet done so to make pledges for 2026 and 2027.

In response, a number of representatives provided information on their countries’ contributions. The representative of Japan announced that his Government would contribute $200,000 for 2026, which was approximately $10,000 more than its pledge for 2025, and would also continue to provide in-kind contributions to the technical support unit for the task force on scenarios and models, which was hosted by the country’s Institute for Global Environmental Strategies. The representative of the United Kingdom, recalling that his Government’s contribution in 2025 had amounted to just over £1.3 million, announced a pledge to the trust fund of £500,000 for 2026.
In addition, the Chair recalled the pledge made by the Government of France, referred to in the country’s opening statement.
The Plenary established a contact group on budget, chaired by Erik Grigoryan (Armenia), to further consider the financial and budgetary arrangements for the Platform.
Subsequently, the Chair of the contact group on budget reported that the group had reached consensus on all the matters under discussion.
A representative of the secretariat presented a draft decision on the matter and drew attention to the need for a minor editorial amendment to the text as presented.
The Plenary adopted decision IPBES-12/3 on financial and budgetary arrangements. The decision is set out in the annex to the present report.

division.heading: Assessing knowledge: methodological assessment of the impact and dependence of business on biodiversity and nature’s contributions to people

content.p: Introducing the item, the Chair drew attention to the summary for policymakers of the business and biodiversity assessment (IPBES/12/6), the chapters of the assessment (IPBES/12/INF/1) and the overview of the process followed for the preparation of the assessment (IPBES/12/INF/5). He expressed deep appreciation to the Co-Chairs of the assessment for their time and dedication over the previous three years and, through them, to the many experts who had also contributed a significant amount of time and effort.

The Plenary agreed to request working group I to consider the summary for policymakers, working on the basis of the Chair’s informal note on the matter and the proposed draft decision set out in document IPBES/12/1/Add.2. The working group was to be co-chaired by Eeva Primmer (Finland) and Floyd Homer (Trinidad and Tobago).

Subsequently, the Plenary considered the draft summary for policymakers of the business and biodiversity assessment, which the working group had prepared, and a draft decision on the matter, in which the Plenary would approve the summary for policymakers, as revised by the working group, and accept the chapters of the assessment, including their executive summaries.

During the ensuing discussion, the Chair informed participants that, owing to the late conclusion of the working group’s deliberations the previous night, parts of the draft summary for policymakers were available in English only. He emphasized that any editorial issues that remained unresolved in the English version of the document would be duly amended.

Several representatives requested confirmation that the relevant documents would be made available in all official languages of the United Nations following the closure of the session. One representative requested information on mechanisms for avoiding situations in which the Plenary, during future sessions, made decisions on the basis of documents not yet available in all official languages. Another representative requested confirmation that the errors in two of the figures in the summary for policymakers would be corrected.

The Chair, saying that every effort was made to ensure the timely translation of all documents during sessions of the Plenary, noted that participants could assist in that endeavour by ensuring that the Plenary concluded its business in the swiftest time possible. He confirmed that the relevant documents would be made available in all official United Nations languages.

The Co-Chairs of the business and biodiversity assessment delivered statements in which they reflected on the challenging process of producing the assessment report, which had taken several years; reaffirmed the importance of the assessment as an aid for businesses in taking positive action for nature, including in the global South; and thanked all the stakeholders, authors, experts and technical support staff whose dedicated work, in the spirit of multilateralism, had produced an assessment that would contribute to the achievement of a fairer and more sustainable future.

The Plenary adopted decision IPBES-12/1 on the implementation of the rolling work programme of IPBES up to 2030, including part II thereof, entitled "Assessing knowledge", in which, among other things, it approved the summary for policymakers of the business and biodiversity assessment and accepted the individual chapters of the assessment, including their executive summaries. The decision is set out in the annex to the present report.

During the subsequent discussion, a number of representatives expressed gratitude to all those who had participated in producing the business and biodiversity assessment, while others congratulated participants on their work on the assessment during the session.

division.heading: Building capacity, strengthening knowledge foundations and supporting policy

content.p: Introducing the item, the Chair drew attention to the note by the secretariat on work on building capacity, strengthening knowledge foundations and supporting policy (IPBES/12/7), in which workplans for the implementation of objectives 2, 3 and 4 of the rolling work programme up to 2030 were set out for the period between the twelfth and thirteenth sessions. Information on the work carried out by the task forces during the intersessional period preceding the current session was set out in documents IPBES/12/INF/10–IPBES/12/INF/16.

He expressed appreciation to the members of the Multidisciplinary Expert Panel, the Bureau and the task force who had contributed to the work on those important functions of IPBES, as well as to the technical support units, which had ably supported the work.

The Plenary agreed to request working group II to consider the item, working on the basis of the Chair’s informal note on the matter and the proposed draft decision set out in document IPBES/12/1/Add.2. The working group was to be co-chaired by Hesiquio Benítez Díaz (Mexico) and Sebastian König (Switzerland).

The Plenary adopted decision IPBES-12/1 on the implementation of the rolling work programme of IPBES up to 2030, as orally amended, including parts III, IV, V and VII thereof, entitled "Building capacity", "Strengthening the knowledge foundations", "Supporting policy", and "Technical support for the work programme", respectively, pertaining to, among other things, the workplans of the attendant task forces for the intersessional period. The decision is set out in the annex to the present report.

division.heading: Improving the effectiveness of the Platform

content.p: Introducing the item, the Chair recalled that an initial review of IPBES had been conducted at the end of the first work programme of the Platform, with the outcomes of the review being presented to the Plenary at its seventh session, in 2019, and considered in the development of the rolling work programme of the Platform up to 2030. The rolling work programme comprised six objectives, with the sixth being improving the effectiveness of the Platform. Under objective 6 (a), a periodic review of the effectiveness of IPBES was foreseen, including a midterm and a final review.

In decision IPBES-10/1, the Plenary had approved terms of reference for the midterm review, which would include an internal part and an external part. The internal part of the review had been conducted by the Bureau and the Multidisciplinary Expert Panel between the tenth and eleventh sessions, and their report had been presented to the Plenary at its eleventh session.

For the external part of the midterm review, the Plenary had requested a review panel, comprising 15 members nominated by Governments and selected by the Bureau, to conduct the review between the eleventh and twelfth sessions. The full report of the external review panel was set out in document IPBES/12/INF/20, with a summary of the report, including the specific recommendations for the further implementation of the rolling work programme up to 2030, contained in annex II to document IPBES/12/8.
An overview of responses by the Bureau, the Multidisciplinary Expert Panel and the Executive Secretary to the recommendations developed by the review panel were set out in document IPBES/12/INF/21.

He expressed deep appreciation to the Co-Chairs of the review panel, Ntakadzeni Tshidada (South Africa) and Andrew Stott (United Kingdom), all members of the review panel, and Boris Božić, the consultant supporting the review, for their efforts in completing the midterm review in time for the current session.
The Plenary agreed to request working group II to consider the item, including consideration of the proposed draft decision on the matter set out in document IPBES/12/1/Add.2.

Subsequently, the Plenary considered a draft decision on the matter. One representative suggested that the draft decision should refer to requesting, rather than encouraging, the Bureau, the Multidisciplinary Expert Panel and the Executive Secretary to continue implementing those recommendations of the midterm review that supported the implementation of the existing mandates, within available resources.

The Plenary adopted decision IPBES-12/1 on the implementation of the rolling work programme of IPBES up to 2030, as orally amended, including part VI thereof, entitled "Improving the effectiveness of the Platform". The decision is set out in the annex to the present report.

division.heading: Requests, input and suggestions for additional elements of the rolling work programme of the Platform up to 2030

content.p: Introducing the item, the Chair recalled that, in decision IPBES-7/1, the Plenary had adopted the rolling work programme of the Platform up to 2030, which had included an initial set of priority topics. In the same decision, the Plenary had recognized the need for ongoing adaptive management of the Platform, according to evolving needs and priorities, and had allowed for the consideration of adjustments to the schedule and list of assessments, as necessary.

In decision IPBES-10/1, the Plenary had requested the Executive Secretary to issue a call for further requests, input and suggestions following the eleventh session of the Plenary, and had decided to determine, at its twelfth session, the exact topic for a further assessment up to 2030. The report by the Bureau and the Multidisciplinary Expert Panel on the prioritization of the requests, input and suggestions received in response to the call issued by the Executive Secretary was set out in document IPBES/12/9/Add.1, and an overview of the requests, input and suggestions received was set out in document IPBES/12/INF/22.

In addition, the Bureau and the Multidisciplinary Expert Panel had reflected on the outcomes of the midterm review under the rolling work programme, the financial situation of the Platform, and recent experiences of implementing the rolling work programme. Strategic considerations regarding the future work of IPBES and a recommendation by the Bureau and the Panel on a way forward were set out in document IPBES/12/9.

The Plenary agreed to request working group II to consider the item, including consideration of the proposed draft decision set out in document IPBES/12/1/Add.2. Additional information was available in the Chair’s informal note on the matter.
Subsequently, the Plenary considered a draft decision on the matter.

The Plenary adopted decision IPBES-12/1 on the implementation of the rolling work programme of IPBES up to 2030, as orally amended, including part II thereof, entitled "Assessing knowledge". The decision is set out in the annex to the present report.

division.heading: Organization of the Plenary; dates and venues of future sessions of the Plenary

content.p: Introducing the item, the Chair recalled that, in decision IPBES-11/2, the Plenary had decided that the thirteenth session would be held in the second half of 2026, taking into account the calendar of relevant international meetings, and had invited members of the Platform in a position to do so to consider hosting that session.

The Bureau, at its twenty-third meeting, held in April 2025, had discussed the logistical and budgetary challenges arising from the organization of two Plenary sessions in 2026 and, following consultations with members, had decided to recommend that the Plenary further consider, at its twelfth session, the dates and venue of its thirteenth session, with a view to holding that session in the second half of 2027, and that the Plenary consider both the monitoring assessment and the spatial planning and connectivity assessment at that session. It was envisaged that the thirteenth session would be held over seven days in October or November 2027.

Relevant information, including a draft provisional agenda and organization of work for the thirteenth and fourteenth sessions, was set out in the note by the secretariat on the organization of work of the Plenary and the dates and venues of future sessions of the Plenary (IPBES/12/10). Noting that the secretariat had not yet received any offers to host the thirteenth session, he invited Governments interested in hosting the session to contact the secretariat as soon as possible.

Subsequently, as no offer to host the thirteenth session had been received, the Plenary agreed to request that the secretariat prepare a draft decision establishing only the general time frame for the thirteenth and fourteenth sessions and mandating the Bureau to decide within the following six months on the venue of the thirteenth session.
One representative, noting that one of the meetings of working group I during the current session had been held in English only, requested that such practices be avoided at future sessions.
In response, the Chair said that every effort would be taken to avoid such situations in future.

One representative expressed support for the proposals that the Plenary consider, at its thirteenth session, the monitoring assessment and the spatial planning and connectivity assessment, and that the thirteenth session be held early in the second half of 2027. He also expressed support for the proposals that the Plenary consider the second global assessment at its fourteenth session, and that that session be held in the second half of 2028, preferably prior to the eighteenth meeting of the Conference of the Parties to the Convention on Biological Diversity.

Subsequently, the Plenary considered a draft decision on the matter. One representative, noting that no firm offers had yet been received to host the thirteenth and fourteenth sessions of the Plenary, proposed that a silence procedure, through national focal points, be implemented to ensure that any decision on the matter was arrived at through an inclusive and participatory process. The Plenary decided that the modalities set out in the draft decision for deciding on the dates and venues of the thirteenth and fourteenth sessions were in accordance with the rules of procedure of the Plenary, and that the provision that the Bureau would decide on the dates and venues of the session in close consultation with the members of the Platform accommodated the proposal of the representative.

In response to concerns raised by some representatives, the Plenary agreed to include in the draft decision a paragraph emphasizing that all representatives of members performing functions in connection with the thirteenth and fourteenth sessions of the Plenary should have the right of unimpeded entry into and exit from the host country, and that visas and entry permits, when required, should be granted as speedily as possible and without discrimination.
The Plenary also agreed that the draft provisional agendas for the thirteenth and fourteenth sessions of the Plenary be set out in annexes to the decision.

The Plenary adopted decision IPBES-12/2 on the organization of the Plenary and dates and venues of future sessions of the Plenary, as orally amended. The decision is set out in the annex to the present report.

division.heading: Institutional arrangements: United Nations collaborative partnership arrangement for the work of the Platform and its secretariat

content.p: Introducing the item, the Chair recalled that, in its decision IPBES-2/8, the Plenary had approved a collaborative partnership arrangement to establish an institutional link between the Plenary of the Platform and UNEP, UNESCO, FAO and UNDP, as set out in the annex to the decision.

A representative of FAO, speaking on behalf of the four United Nations system partners of IPBES, presented the progress report on the United Nations collaborative partnership arrangement (IPBES/12/INF/23).

The Chair expressed his appreciation to UNEP, UNESCO, FAO and UNDP for the support that they had provided to the Platform and asked them to continue to provide such support during the coming intersessional period.

division.heading: Adoption of the decisions and the report of the session

content.p: The Plenary adopted decisions IPBES-12/1–IPBES-12/3, as set out in the annex to the present report.

The Plenary adopted the present report on the basis of the draft report that had been circulated, on the understanding that the report would be finalized by the secretariat under the supervision of the Bureau.

division.heading: Closure of the session

content.p: Following the customary exchange of courtesies, the Chair declared the session closed at 2.20 p.m. on 8 February 2026.

content.p: The task force on capacity-building, whose members were selected following the tenth session of the Plenary of the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services (IPBES) and will serve until the end of the thirteenth session of the Plenary, will oversee and take part in the implementation of the present workplan, supported by the technical support unit for capacity-building at the Norwegian Environment Agency.

division.heading: Objective 2 (a): enhanced learning and engagement

p.i: Deliverable: implementation of the fellowship programme

intro.p: Activities for the implementation of the fellowship programme will include:

content.p: Provision of support for the participation of fellows in the second author meeting of the methodological assessment on monitoring biodiversity and nature’s contributions to people (monitoring assessment), the second author meeting of the methodological assessment of integrated biodiversity-inclusive spatial planning and ecological connectivity (spatial planning and connectivity assessment), and the second and third author meetings of the second global assessment of biodiversity and ecosystem services;

Organization of an annual training workshop for fellows in ongoing assessments and in the task force on scenarios and models. The workshop will enhance the capacity of fellows regarding key topics relevant to their activities in IPBES and provide an opportunity for them to engage with and learn from each other, both within and between the various cohorts of fellows;
Working with the IPBES fellows and alumni network and organizing an online meeting for the network.

p.i: Deliverable: implementation of the training and familiarization programme

intro.p: Activities for the implementation of the training and familiarization programme for IPBES experts and others involved in the science-policy interface will include:

content.p: Further development and promotion of IPBES webinars, online tools and videos on approved IPBES assessment reports and other products;

Further provision of (non-financial) support for relevant training activities tailored to IPBES needs, catalysed by IPBES and developed by other organizations and institutions (e.g., in the form of printed or electronic materials, feedback on draft agendas or contact details for relevant IPBES experts);

Organization of a youth workshop aimed at strengthening the engagement of young people in the work of IPBES and at supporting the uptake of assessments among young people, other individuals and organizations, subject to the availability of resources.
The workshop will target individuals representing youth organizations from different United Nations regions that have an active voice in their respective communities. An open call, including selection criteria, will be issued.

p.i: Deliverable: organization of science-policy dialogues with national focal points

content.p:
Activities to further enhance the capacity of Governments to participate in the development of ongoing IPBES assessments and other work programme deliverables and to use completed IPBES assessments, including the knowledge gaps identified therein, and other IPBES work in policymaking and decision-making will include an in-person dialogue meeting with national focal points and an online meeting for new IPBES national focal points and other government representatives.
The dialogue meeting with national focal points will include discussions on topics such as recommendations and implementation options directed to national focal points and identified in the midterm review, as well as options for further supporting the use and uptake of IPBES products.

intro.p: Online dialogues in support of external reviews will be organized:

content.p: With Governments and stakeholders in support of the external reviews of the spatial planning and connectivity assessment and the second global assessment;
With Governments in support of the additional government reviews of the monitoring assessment and the spatial planning and connectivity assessment.

division.heading: Objective 2 (b): facilitated access to expertise and information

p.i: Deliverable: support for the uptake of approved assessment reports and other deliverables, and encouragement of the development of communities of practice around them

intro.p: Activities to support the uptake of approved assessment findings and other deliverables at all levels and to encourage the development of communities of practice around them will include:

content.p: Issuance of a call to members and other organizations to support the uptake of approved IPBES assessment reports and other products (e.g., e-learning tools), and provision of support for such activities (e.g., in the form of printed or electronic materials, feedback on draft agendas, or contact details for relevant IPBES experts);
Further encouragement of communities of practice to facilitate access to expertise and information relevant to IPBES;

Collaboration with the other task forces in catalysing activities to further build capacity in relation to IPBES approaches and processes, including the approach to recognizing and working with Indigenous and local knowledge in IPBES.

p.i: Deliverable: convening of regular meetings of the capacity-building forum

content.p: A ninth meeting of the capacity-building forum will be convened online to facilitate engagement with, and to build and further enhance collaboration among, organizations and institutions for the implementation of the IPBES rolling capacity-building plan. The specific theme of the forum will be proposed by the task force on capacity-building and agreed on by the Bureau.

division.heading: Objective 2 (c): strengthened national and regional capacities

p.i: Deliverable: encouragement of the development of science-policy platforms, networks and assessments for biodiversity and ecosystem services at the national and (sub)regional levels

content.p: The task force will continue to encourage, collaborate with and strengthen national and (sub)regional science-policy platforms and networks for biodiversity and ecosystem services. Activities will focus on facilitating the sharing of knowledge and best practices among existing national and (sub)regional science-policy platforms, those interested in establishing new platforms, and organizations and institutions that could support such efforts. An online dialogue workshop will be organized as part of this work.

Provision of scientific support for the development of the IPBES semantic knowledge base, and technical support for the establishment and maintenance of the associated triple store.

For the methodological assessment of the impact and dependence of business on biodiversity and nature’s contributions to people (business and biodiversity assessment), provision of support on aspects relating to the completion, documenting and archiving of the work carried out during the development of the assessment;

intro.p: For the methodological assessment on monitoring biodiversity and nature’s contributions to people (monitoring assessment), the methodological assessment of integrated biodiversity-inclusive spatial planning and ecological connectivity (spatial planning and connectivity assessment) and the second global assessment of biodiversity and ecosystem services, technical support for:

content.p: The implementation of the data and knowledge management policy, in line with the roles set out in the policy;

Performing systematic literature searches and analyses, applying natural language processing, handling computationally demanding data sets and providing access to high-performance computing facilities and advanced data technologies;
The analysis and creation of spatial data, as well as the verification of maps for conformity with the IPBES guidelines;
Access to, handling of and, if needed, processing of external data and knowledge for use in the assessments, as well as the use of data and knowledge services offered by external entities;
Ensuring that IPBES products are available in structured formats that can be processed by digital tools to facilitate their integration and use by Governments and stakeholders.

content.p: The Multidisciplinary Expert Panel and the Bureau will oversee and take part, within the scope of their respective mandates, in the implementation of the present workplan for the component on knowledge generation catalysis of objective 3 (a), supported by the technical support unit for knowledge generation catalysis hosted by the French Biodiversity Agency with support from the Ministry of Ecological Transition and Territorial Cohesion of France on behalf of the Biodiversa+ European Biodiversity Partnership.

The Multidisciplinary Expert Panel and the Bureau will conduct activities to ensure the effective implementation of the workplan, including the continued monitoring of a set of relevant indicators (see annex VII).

p.i: Deliverable: provision of support to assessment authors in identifying knowledge gaps, including in producing a list of knowledge gaps as part of the assessments, using the guidelines and template

content.p: Activities to support assessment experts in the identification of knowledge gaps will include the provision of technical support in the process of knowledge gap identification and the presentation and collection of such gaps by the technical support units of the respective assessments and by the secretariat, with input on the identification and presentation of knowledge gaps from the technical support unit for knowledge generation catalysis.

p.i: Deliverable: promotion of actions by relevant external organizations and initiatives to address identified knowledge gaps

intro.p: Activities to enhance communication and outreach to catalyse the generation of new knowledge will include:

content.p: Development of communication materials that will be available on the website of the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services (IPBES), including a dedicated fact sheet and a set of presentations on the gaps identified in the methodological assessment of the impact and dependence of business on biodiversity and nature’s contributions to people (business and biodiversity assessment) that can be made publicly available for use by members, observers and stakeholders;

intro.p: Organization of dialogue meetings to present the knowledge gaps identified in the business and biodiversity assessment, as follows:

content.p: With research funding agencies and other relevant funding organizations, with particular emphasis on areas where additional research investment is crucial;

With Governments, by inviting IPBES national focal points to extend the invitation to relevant representatives of their countries, including national focal points for relevant multilateral environmental agreements, with emphasis on gaps of particular policy relevance for national or international processes;
With researchers, academia and other stakeholders;

intro.p: Provision of input for presenting the knowledge gaps identified in the business and biodiversity assessment for activities organized by other task forces, as follows:

content.p: On Indigenous and local knowledge-related knowledge gaps for relevant activities organized by the task force on Indigenous and local knowledge;
On identified knowledge gaps for IPBES activities related to the engagement of youth;
Further development of the online database of identified knowledge gaps with regard to the inclusion of recently completed assessments and its user interface and functionalities;
Identification of recurring knowledge gaps or common themes among knowledge gaps from multiple completed assessments to support communication efforts;
Continued preparation for the identification of general knowledge needs as part of future scoping processes.

p.i: Deliverable: monitoring of the impact of knowledge generation catalysis efforts to effectively fill the identified gaps

intro.p: Activities to ensure the overall coherence, efficiency and regular updating of the knowledge generation catalysis process will include:

content.p: Seeking the views of research funding agencies and other relevant funding organizations on the ways in which knowledge gaps identified in completed IPBES assessments are documented and communicated by IPBES, and collecting information on the different types of research funding agencies and other funding organizations relevant to IPBES work on knowledge generation catalysis, both through conducting an online survey and as part of the online meetings organized under the present workplan;

Developing, with due attention to the information collected through the activities set out in subparagraph (a) above and the outcomes of the midterm review under the IPBES rolling work programme up to 2030, a concept note with reflections on the progress, outcomes and limitations of the current knowledge generation catalysis process and on elements to strengthen the process, as input to the deliberations of the Multidisciplinary Expert Panel and the Bureau regarding the future work of the Platform.

Efforts will be made to collect information on initiatives that contribute to the generation of new knowledge in response to the knowledge gaps identified by IPBES, in close coordination with work on data and knowledge management. This will include a call for information on any contributions to the generation of new knowledge, addressing the identified knowledge gaps in completed IPBES assessments, and engagement with relevant international scientific journals by inviting them to notify IPBES when new research articles are submitted that address the knowledge gaps identified in completed IPBES assessments. The information collected will be made available on the IPBES website.
https://www.ipbes.net/knowledge-gaps-questionnaire-2025/results. Relevant submissions addressing the identified knowledge gaps will also be linked to the online database mentioned in paragraph 4 (d) above.

attachment.subheading: Workplan for objective 3 (b): enhanced recognition of and work with Indigenous and local knowledge systems, for the intersessional period until the thirteenth session of the Plenary

FRBRalias.value: Annex IV to decision IPBES-12/1 Workplan for objective 3 (b): enhanced recognition of and work with Indigenous and local knowledge systems, for the intersessional period until the thirteenth session of the Plenary
FRBRalias.name: title

content.p: The task force on Indigenous and local knowledge, whose members were selected following the tenth session of the Plenary of the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services (IPBES) and will serve until the end of the thirteenth session of the Plenary, will oversee and take part in the implementation of the present workplan for objective 3 (b), supported by the technical support unit for Indigenous and local knowledge at the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization.
The task force will conduct activities to ensure the effective implementation of the workplan, including the continued monitoring of a set of relevant indicators (see annex VII).

p.i: Deliverable: implementation of the approach to recognizing and working with Indigenous and local knowledge in IPBES

intro.p: Activities for the implementation of the approach to recognizing and working with Indigenous and local knowledge in IPBES will include:

content.p: Support for Indigenous and local knowledge liaison groups for ongoing assessments, including the provision of capacity-building and training on recognizing and working with Indigenous and local knowledge and on using multiple types of evidence on Indigenous and local knowledge in assessments and in identifying gaps relating to Indigenous and local knowledge;
A call for contributions for the second global assessment of biodiversity and ecosystem services;

Dialogue workshops with experts on Indigenous and local knowledge and with members of Indigenous Peoples and local communities (in person, hybrid or online) for the external reviews of the methodological assessment of integrated biodiversity-inclusive spatial planning and ecological connectivity (spatial planning and connectivity assessment) and the second global assessment;

During the external reviews of the spatial planning and connectivity assessment and the second global assessment: review of the drafts by the task force; dissemination of the invitation to review through relevant networks, partly with the aim of mobilizing additional relevant Indigenous and local knowledge; and provision of support regarding Indigenous and local knowledge-related content for the dialogue organized by the task force on capacity-building;

intro.p: Post-assessment activities, conducted in close coordination with activities under capacity-building, knowledge generation catalysis and policy support:

content.p: Collation and dissemination of materials of relevance to Indigenous Peoples and local communities from the report on the methodological assessment of the impact and dependence of business on biodiversity and nature’s contributions to people (business and biodiversity assessment), in all six official languages of the United Nations, including their dissemination to national and regional platforms on biodiversity and ecosystem services and to Indigenous Peoples and local communities;

Webinar to communicate the key messages of relevance to Indigenous Peoples and local communities from the business and biodiversity assessment to a broad audience, including Indigenous Peoples and local communities;

Provision of support for the development of materials from completed IPBES assessments by other organizations and institutions, and for related uptake and outreach activities by other organizations and institutions;
Support for the communication of Indigenous and local knowledge mobilization gaps identified in completed IPBES assessments;
Provision of support for the work of other task forces regarding aspects related to Indigenous and local knowledge;

Further development of the methodological guidance on the implementation of the approach to recognizing and working with Indigenous and local knowledge in IPBES, based on experience from completed and ongoing assessments and on the activities described in the present workplan, with a focus on enhancing the dialogue within IPBES between Indigenous and local knowledge systems and science;
Webinar on methods for working with Indigenous and local knowledge in different environmental assessment processes;

Continuation of the review of the implementation of the approach to recognizing and working with Indigenous and local knowledge in IPBES to include experiences from the business and biodiversity assessment.

p.i: Deliverable: strengthening the implementation of the participatory mechanism

intro.p: Activities for strengthening the implementation of the participatory mechanism will include:

content.p: Continued collaboration with the Multidisciplinary Expert Panel in the implementation of the participatory mechanism, including consideration of the results of the review of the implementation of the approach to recognizing and working with Indigenous and local knowledge in IPBES, carried out in the previous intersessional period;

Engagement with and capacity-building for Indigenous Peoples and local communities through seminars and side events at relevant meetings, both online and in person, in order to inform Indigenous Peoples and local communities about the work of IPBES and about opportunities for participation, to enhance the benefits they receive from that work and to stimulate discussion and contributions of Indigenous and local knowledge;
Further development of the Indigenous and local knowledge section of the IPBES website for improved usability and display of information.

attachment.heading: Annex V to decision IPBES-12/1
attachment.subheading: Workplan for objective 4 (a): advanced work on policy instruments, policy support tools and methodologies, for the intersessional period until the thirteenth session of the Plenary

FRBRalias.value: Annex V to decision IPBES-12/1 Workplan for objective 4 (a): advanced work on policy instruments, policy support tools and methodologies, for the intersessional period until the thirteenth session of the Plenary
FRBRalias.name: title

content.p: The Multidisciplinary Expert Panel and the Bureau, within the scope of their respective mandates, will oversee and take part in the implementation of the present workplan for objective 4 (a), supported by the technical support unit for policy support at the United Nations Environment Programme World Conservation Monitoring Centre. Activities related to engagement with multilateral environmental agreements, other intergovernmental processes and relevant international organizations will be carried out by the secretariat of the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services (IPBES).

The Multidisciplinary Expert Panel and the Bureau will conduct activities to ensure the effective implementation of the workplan, including the continued monitoring of a set of relevant indicators (see annex VII).

p.i: Deliverable: strengthening of the policy relevance of IPBES assessments and provision of support to authors of the policy chapters in IPBES assessment reports

intro.p: Activities for ensuring that IPBES assessment reports and other products are policy relevant will include:

content.p: Provision of training to experts of the second global assessment of biodiversity and ecosystem services in the process and requirements of policymaking in order to strengthen their awareness of the policy landscape, including multilateral environmental agreements, and its relevance to the assessment, their understanding of how to frame content in an accessible and understandable manner for policy audiences, and their capacity to use the methodological guidance for assessing policy instruments, policy tools and methodologies;

Review of the chapters that set out policy options and of the summary for policymakers during the external reviews of the methodological assessment of integrated biodiversity-inclusive spatial planning and ecological connectivity (spatial planning and connectivity assessment) and the second global assessment;

Encouragement of the participation of policy experts, experts on science-policy interfaces, practitioners and knowledge holders in the external reviews of drafts of the spatial planning and connectivity assessment and second global assessment, through targeted outreach.

p.i: Deliverables: promotion of and support for the use of findings of IPBES products in decision-making

intro.p: Activities for supporting the use of completed IPBES assessment reports and other IPBES products by decision makers in all relevant sectors will include:

content.p: Working with the co-chairs and the technical support unit in the development of draft fact sheets for the methodological assessment on monitoring biodiversity and nature’s contributions to people (monitoring assessment) and the spatial planning and connectivity assessment, including consideration of multilateral environmental agreement-specific fact sheets, to be finalized after the thirteenth session of the Plenary and to be made available on the IPBES website;

Engagement, by the secretariat, with the secretariats of relevant multilateral environmental agreements, other intergovernmental processes and relevant international organizations to inform them about the assessments in preparation and about the findings of completed assessments, as appropriate;

Coordination, by the secretariat, of the involvement of relevant experts to provide information about the assessments in preparation and about the findings of completed assessments to relevant bodies of multilateral environmental agreements, other intergovernmental processes and relevant international organizations;

Development, by the technical support units of completed assessments, in coordination with the secretariat, of presentations and materials for use by IPBES members, observers and other stakeholders, with the presentations to be made available on the IPBES website;

Holding a global online dialogue with IPBES national focal points and a dialogue with stakeholders to share experiences in using IPBES assessment reports in policymaking and decision-making at the regional, national and subnational levels, with a focus on the policy options identified in recently completed assessment reports and including information of relevance to Indigenous Peoples and local communities and its use in the context of policymaking, and to encourage them to report on those experiences in the IPBES impact-tracking database (TRACK), to enable an understanding of the activities carried out and better evaluation of impacts;

Working with the task force on data and knowledge management to pilot and refine the approaches developed or identified for systematically tracking the impact of IPBES assessments, including their use in laws, regulations, policies, decisions, commitments, investments, networks, initiatives, ideas, research, techniques and educational materials, identifying the reasons, opportunities and barriers involved in taking account of IPBES outputs, and developing recommendations or suggestions for overcoming barriers in that regard;
Development of a concept note outlining options for more effective contextualization of the findings of IPBES assessments for specific audiences;
Working with the task force on capacity-building to enhance the sharing of good-practice case studies for supporting the uptake of IPBES assessments;

Working with the technical support unit on data and knowledge management to identify ways in which data and knowledge generated in the second global assessment could be communicated through interactive online tools, and developing a proposal for further work in this area.

The Executive Secretary will issue a notification, also in support of IPBES work on capacity-building, inviting IPBES members, observers and other stakeholders to carry out activities that support the uptake and impact of completed IPBES assessment reports and other products.

FRBRalias.value: Annex VI to decision IPBES-12/1 Workplan for objective 4 (b): advanced work on scenarios and models of biodiversity and ecosystem functions and services, for the intersessional period until the thirteenth session of the Plenary
